summary: Standards-track Telnet option that lets a client and server exchange the type of terminal in use, so the server can format output properly. It supersedes RFC 930, and adds the ability to cycle through a list of possible terminal types to select the most appropriate one.

eli5.summary: A computer far away needs to know what kind of screen you have. This lets your computer say what it is, and offer a list so the other side can pick one it understands.

questions: how does telnet negotiate terminal type
what is the telnet terminal type option

subtitle: How a Telnet client tells the server what kind of terminal it is, and offers a list of alternatives to pick from.

tldr.problem: A Telnet client that can emulate several terminals needs a way to present them all to the server, and to change emulation mid-session. Older mechanisms treated multiple names as synonyms and could scan the list only once.
tldr.mechanism: After the usual WILL/DO negotiation of option 24, the server sends SEND sub-negotiations and the client answers with IS plus a terminal type name. Repeated requests walk through the client's list, and repeating a name signals the end of the list.
tldr.outcome: It supersedes RFC 930 and stays backward compatible with it. It is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes it.

today: RFC 1091 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 930, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Terminal Types Need a List
sections.content:
Many bit-mapped displays, such as PCs and graphics workstations, run a client program that imitates a conventional ASCII terminal. Most of these programs have several emulation modes with widely varying characteristics, and modern host software can deal with many terminal types.

What is needed, says RFC 1091, is a way for the client to present a list of its emulation modes so the server can choose the one it prefers, plus a way to change modes during a session. Existing Telnet mechanisms were not built for this: multiple names are assumed to be synonyms, mode changes are not defined, and the list can only be scanned once.

The document is a simple extension of those mechanisms. It makes one assumption about implementations of the previous standard, RFC 930, to stay fully backward compatible.
sections.eli5: A computer far away wants to know what kind of screen you have. Your computer may be able to pretend to be several kinds, so it needs a way to share the whole list.

sections.title: The Option and Its Commands
sections.content:
The option is called TERMINAL-TYPE and has the code 24. Willingness is agreed with ordinary Telnet option negotiation: IAC WILL TERMINAL-TYPE means the sender will send terminal type information in a later sub-negotiation, and IAC DO TERMINAL-TYPE means the sender is willing to receive it. WON'T and DON'T are the refusals.

The default is WON'T and DON'T, so no terminal type information is exchanged unless both sides agree. WILL and DO only grant permission; the real exchange happens inside option subcommands.

Two subcommands carry the data. IAC SB TERMINAL-TYPE SEND IAC SE (code 1) is the server asking the client for its next terminal type. IAC SB TERMINAL-TYPE IS ... IAC SE (code 0) is the client stating its current terminal type name.
sections.eli5: First both sides say 'yes, let us talk about screens.' Then one side asks 'what are you?' and the other side answers with a name.

sections.title: Who Asks and Who Answers
sections.content:
Once a WILL and a DO have been exchanged, the sender of the DO, the server, is free to request type information. The specification is deliberately asymmetric: only the server may send requests, and only the client may send type information. Type information is never sent spontaneously, only in response to a request.

The type is an NVT ASCII string in which upper and lower case are equivalent. The list of valid names is kept in the "Assigned Numbers" RFC, and the maximum length of a terminal type name is 40 characters.

When the client answers, it must at the same time switch its emulation mode to match, unless the name is a synonym of the previous one or another prerequisite (such as agreeing on the Telnet binary option) is not yet met. The server, by contrast, need not change anything on receipt, but it may pass the information to a process, for example a terminal driver, so output can suit the terminal. The reason for the asymmetry is that server operating systems and applications generally cannot change terminal types at arbitrary points in a session.
sections.eli5: The far-away computer is the one who asks, and your computer is the one who answers. Your computer changes how it behaves to match what it just said.

sections.title: Cycling Through the List
sections.content:
A client may know a terminal by several names, such as a specific type and a more generic one, or may be able to emulate several kinds of terminal. It should answer successive SEND requests with the different names. A server that does not understand the first answer can therefore ask again for alternatives. Names that are synonyms should be sent from most to least specific, and the emulator must end up in the mode of the last type sent.

The end of the list is marked by repetition. When the server gets the same response twice in a row, that is the end of the list. The client likewise shows it has sent every name by repeating the last one. If the server asks yet again, it wants to return to the top of the list, 'probably to select the least of N evils.'

This keeps old servers working: servers following the previous standard stop sending SEND after the same response twice. Clients of the old standard are assumed to send the last type on the list in reply to a third query as well as the second, and new-style servers must recognize this and send no more queries. The name UNKNOWN is used when the terminal type is unknown or unlikely to be recognized by the other party.
sections.eli5: If the teacher does not know the first name you say, she asks again and you give another. When you say the same name twice, she knows you have run out. If she asks once more, you start over from your first name.

sections.title: Implementation and User Interface Advice
sections.content:
The terminal type can be any NVT ASCII string meaningful to both ends. The Assigned Numbers list exists to avoid confusion over alternative spellings, for example one side saying IBM3278-2 and the other IBM-3278/2. There is no negative acknowledgement for a type that is not understood, but other options, such as switching to binary mode, may be refused if a valid name was not given.

Clients that support multiple emulation modes should let the user choose, before the connection is made, which mode is preferred, meaning which name is sent first. The order cannot change after negotiation begins, and the initial mode also becomes the default with servers that do not support TERMINAL-TYPE.

Servers should store the current type name and the list of available names where both the user (through a keyboard command) and applications can read them. They should also offer a way to request a change of terminal type by starting a series of SEND/IS sub-negotiations.
sections.eli5: Everyone should spell the names the same way so nobody gets confused. You should be able to choose your favourite name to say first.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three exchanges. In the first, the server finds the first type, IBM-3278-2, acceptable and stops after one request. In the second, an old-style (RFC 930 compatible) exchange, the client answers ZENITH-H19 and then UNKNOWN twice, and the server accepts the second type as the last on the list.

In the third, a new-style client and server, the client offers DEC-VT220, DEC-VT100 and DEC-VT52, then repeats DEC-VT52 to mark the end of the list. The server asks once more and the client wraps around to DEC-VT220, the first type offered.
sections.eli5: In the longest example the teacher keeps asking, hears the whole list, then asks once too often and hears the first answer again.
